title: Redwood discovery - model selection with Veridian Logic
summary: Initial discovery focusing on model selection tradeoffs for a multi-lingual assistant and private deployment constraints. Customer is leaning toward Dedicated or Private due to data residency and latency SLOs; interested in 32k+ context for long dialogs and tool-calling support. Next steps: run benchmarks, share security docs, provide pricing options for Hosted/Dedicated/Private.
action_items: Liam Carter; Send Hosted/Dedicated pricing sheet and example configs; Due: 2026-10-18
Maya Patel; Set up perf benchmark template + request sample prompt set from Marco; Due: 2026-10-20
Dina Park; Share network/VPC requirements and expected QPS; Due: 2026-10-19
next_steps: Redwood to send pricing and deployment matrix (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
Customer to provide representative prompt set and sample documents for perf benchmarks
Schedule a 60-min technical deep-dive with infra team next week
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-15 14:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Liam Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO, Veridian Logic), Marco Reyes (ML Engineer), Dina Park (Infra Lead)

[00:00] Liam: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Liam from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, and with me is Maya, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Aisha: Doing good, thanks. We only have 45-ish minutes, lots to cover.
[00:10] Liam: Great. Quick agenda — model selection and mapping that to hosted, dedicated, and private options; context length and multilingual needs; tool-calling support; security questions; and next steps. Sound okay?
[00:18] Aisha: Yep.
[00:20] Marco: Yeah, let's jump in.
[00:22] Maya: Awesome. Can you give us a brief on your current stack and what you're trying to build?
[00:28] Aisha: Sure. At Veridian Logic we're building a multi-lingual customer assistant for EU and APAC customers, a mix of chat and long-form summarization — so heavy context, long threads, we need about 32k tokens ideally, sometimes up to 64k on special flows. We also need tool-calling to hit internal systems — ticketing, doc retrieval, and some proprietary RAG connectors. Latency matters — we want sub-600ms 95th pct for short prompts, but for long context flows we can tolerate more.
[00:52] Liam: Great, that helps. Two immediate things — context length and tooling. On context length, Redwood supports model variants with 16k, 32k and 64k contexts depending on the open model you pick and hosting mode. For hosted API we have curated open models with verified profiles; for Dedicated you can pin a model variant and get more predictable latency. For Private we do a customer-managed control plane and can support on-prem or VPC with full key management.
[01:16] Marco: When you say "curated open models" which ones are you referring to? Any specific recommendations for multilingual?
[01:21] Maya: Sure — in our catalog we often recommend m-llama2 variants for cost-sensitive ops, but for multilingual and instruction following we often point teams at models like Mistral-XL variants or Llama 3 forks that have been fine-tuned — sorry, the catalog names can be a bit messy sometimes — and we also profile open models like Starcola? -- (laughs) — I mean Starcoder family for code, but for multilingual we have benchmarks on models that were better than older LLaMA in specific languages.
[01:47] Aisha: Is there support for tool-calling / function calling — i.e., deterministic tool invocation like we get from other providers? We need that tightly integrated.
[01:55] Maya: Yes, Redwood supports structured outputs and function/tool calling patterns. The runtime can route calls and we provide SDK helpers to wire up tool contracts. There are some model-specific behaviors — some models are better at reliably emitting json-shaped function calls; we test that in our evals and surface the probabilities.
[02:12] Dina: From infra — our latency concern is that if we run in Hosted with a regional endpoint, network hops could add jitter. We're more interested in Dedicated or Private if we can get SLA-like consistency. Also data residency — EU data must not leave region.
[02:25] Liam: Totally understand. Dedicated offers reserved GPU pools and predictable throughput; Private gives you customer-managed networking and on-prem if you need air-gapped. For EU residency we can put dedicated capacity or private control plane in a EU region and integrate with your KMS.
[02:39] Marco: For the 32k/64k contexts — is that something we choose at model load time, or is it dependent on the quantization and runtime? We're concerned about memory and cost.
[02:48] Maya: Good question. Context support is both model architecture and runtime configuration dependent. Some open models have native 32k support; for others we enable sliding-window or long-seq kernels in the runtime. There are tradeoffs — larger context increases memory and per-token compute. We use batching and KV caching to optimize cost; Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles to reduce memory while keeping quality.
[03:11] Aisha: Any docs or benchmarks we can see for quality vs quantization — especially for multilingual tasks? Some languages degrade faster under aggressive quantization.
[03:20] Maya: We can share our model-performance spreadsheet and language-specific evals. We'll include both top-line latency/throughput numbers and quality regression notes per quant profile. I'll attach that.
[03:29] Liam: Also to mention — fallback policies. If a high-quality large-context model isn't available we can route to a compatible variant or degrade gracefully; that helps with reliability.
[03:38] Marco: Competitors? Are teams using Anthropic or OpenAI for these workloads?
[03:41] Liam: Some customers use Anthropic/OpenAI for hosted generative endpoints; others prefer open model stacks to control cost. You'll see a mix. We often position Redwood for teams that need control over economics and deployment modes.
[03:52] Aisha: Security: SOC2, audit logs, SSO integration — we need SAML/IdP, RBAC, and KMS integration. Also audit trail for PII access.
[04:02] Maya: We're SOC 2 compliant; for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and provide detailed audit logs and trace hooks. SAML/SSO and RBAC are supported in Console for role-based rules. We'll share the security pack.
[04:15] Dina: Network setup questions — what are the egress requirements for private? We need specifics for firewall rules and peering.
[04:22] Maya: For Private we hand over a network requirements doc; if you want on-prem we can provide offline installers. For VPC we typically require specific ports for control plane telemetry, but data can be routed over private peering — we'll provide the exact CIDR/IP ranges in the doc.
[04:37] Aisha: Timeline-wise — we want a pilot within the next 6 weeks if possible. We need to validate latency and cost assumptions.
[04:44] Liam: Sounds reasonable. Typical path: 1) share pricing and recommended model choices, 2) you provide prompt set + sample docs, 3) we run a perf/quality bench on Dedicated and Hosted for apples-to-apples, 4) do a short pilot. We'll attach the benchmark harness.
[05:00] Marco: One more on tool-calling: we have enterprise connectors that need signed requests; can Redwood's function-calling surface support request signing and pass through identity tokens?
[05:10] Maya: Yes — function call payloads can be enriched with tokens and we can provide middleware patterns in the SDK to sign requests or forward an identity token. For Private deployments you can keep keys on-prem.
[05:21] Aisha: Cost — curious about unit economics. If we go Dedicated for lower latency, what's the incremental cost vs Hosted?
[05:28] Liam: Dedicated has a reserved capacity model — you commit to a pool and get lower per-token cost and predictable throughput. Hosted is usage-based with tiers. We'll send a simple comparison table with examples for your expected QPS and token profile.
[05:41] Marco: Any model licensing concerns if we pick some forked open checkpoint?
[05:45] Maya: We only surface models that are permitted for commercial use in our catalog, and we document license constraints. If you bring your own model to Dedicated/Private, we advise running license review but the runtime can generally host it.
[05:58] Aisha: Great. Can we get a sense of reliability SLOs for Dedicated — like availability and latency percentiles?
[06:04] Liam: Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and latency targets; we'll put the SLA terms in the deck. Hosted also has regionally-backed availability numbers.
[06:12] Dina: For the perf benchmarks — can we measure 95th pct latency for short flows and end-to-end latency for long context? We want both.
[06:19] Maya: Absolutely. Our benchmark harness reports p50/p95/p99 and also end-to-end for multi-turn with context restore. We'll run both Dedicated and Hosted configs.
[06:29] Marco: Any caveats with embeddings/semantic search if we use long contexts? We plan to combine RAG with long-context models.
[06:36] Maya: RAG patterns are common; we recommend using embeddings for retrieval and then a long-context model for final assembly. Caching and prefix caching reduce repeated cost. We'll include a recommended architecture diagram.
[06:48] Aisha: Okay — I think we have what we need. Last question: who will run the pilot on Redwood's side?
[06:53] Liam: Maya will own the technical setup and I'll manage the commercial side. We'll both be points of contact.
[06:58] Aisha: Perfect.
[07:00] Liam: Quick recap of actions — send pricing and model catalog, share security docs, Dina share network details, Marco send prompt set, Maya set up benchmark and run tests. Any objections?
[07:12] Marco: No objections.
[07:13] Dina: Sounds good.
[07:14] Aisha: Good. Thanks everyone.
[07:16] Liam: Great, we'll follow up within 48 hours with the docs and a calendar invite for the deep-dive. Thanks for your time.
[07:21] End of call

Notes: transcription includes some mis-named models and informal shorthand (e.g., "Starcola" mis-transcription), occasional run-ons. References: Redwood model catalog link (shared after call), security pack (shared), benchmark harness link (internal).
